headline_insight: Clients from households with a person with disability were significantly more likely to experience an insured event (26.9% vs 16.1%, p_adj=0.00) yet slightly less likely to submit a claim (36.1% vs 45.2%) \u2014 and across all claimants, 39.0% of women filed a claim after an event compared with 48.7% of men, with "I did not know how to file a claim" cited by roughly a third of non-claimants.
paragraphs: The claims funnel narrows sharply at each stage, and it narrows differently by subgroup. Among all insured respondents, 17.7% of women and 20.7% of men reported experiencing an insured event (n=1,392 and n=565 respectively; not statistically significant after adjustment). Of those who did, 39.0% of women submitted a claim compared with 48.7% of men \u2014 a 9.7 percentage point gap that does not reach statistical significance (p_adj=0.3) but is directionally consistent with the disability finding. Clients in households including a person with disability were significantly more likely to have experienced an insured event at all (26.9% versus 16.1% of non-PWD households, p_adj=0.00, n=453 and 1,499), which is unsurprising given higher health-related exposure, yet they were somewhat less likely to convert that event into a claim (36.1% versus 45.2%, not significant). In other words, the groups with the greatest need are not the groups making the most use of the product. Benchmark data is not available for this indicator, so these figures should be read as internal baselines rather than performance against an external standard.

The dominant reason for not claiming is informational, not procedural. Among the 150 women and 60 men who experienced an event but did not claim, 30.7% of women and 38.3% of men said they did not know how to file a claim, while only 2.7% and 3.3% respectively cited a cumbersome process and effectively nobody cited a low benefit (0.7% of women, 0% of men). A further 36.7% of women said they were not covered at the time. Client voices sharpen this picture: a female client in Zambia said simply, \"I did not know about insurance,\" and another in the same country said, \"Because I did not know about anything.\" A female client in Ghana described a different failure \u2014 not her own knowledge but the response she received: \"l told the officer the he did nothing about it.\" The programming implication is direct: the binding constraint on claims utilisation is awareness and frontline follow-through at the moment of loss, not product design or benefit adequacy. Reminder touchpoints at renewal, and a defined officer obligation to initiate the claim conversation when a client reports a life event, would address the largest single leak in the funnel.

The evidence pack flags a genuine divergence between outcome and experience, and it deserves to be named rather than smoothed over. Outcomes are broadly good and broadly gender-equal: 37.5% of female claimants and 38.6% of male claimants had claims approved and paid, with a further 24.0% and 21.1% approved but not yet paid, and rejection rates of only 15.6% and 14.0%. Yet 56.2% of women and 54.4% of men who claimed reported experiencing challenges in the process \u2014 meaning the majority of clients whose claims were ultimately honoured still found the journey difficult. Among PWD-household claimants the challenge rate was higher still at 63.6% versus 52.3%, though with only 44 PWD claimants this is directional and illustrative rather than statistically robust. Notably, 15.6% of female claimants and 15.9% of PWD-household claimants did not know the outcome of their own claim.

The qualitative material explains what \"challenge\" means in practice, and it clusters around communication and guidance rather than paperwork. A female client in Rwanda said, \"I didn't get full guidance and support on the documents submitted,\" and another reported, \"I wasn't know that my grandchild is not supposed to get medical care from my insurance\" \u2014 a coverage-scope misunderstanding discovered only at the point of claim. A female client in Uganda described the silence that follows submission: \"She shared her documents with the officer, but there has been no feedback from him or the insurance providers.\" A female client in Malawi asked plainly, \"I want the officer to come and help us to process the insurance claims because she promised to assist us.\" These accounts sit alongside very low structured challenge codes \u2014 only 1.6% of women and 3.4% of men network-wide flagged difficulty knowing claim status \u2014 which suggests the closed-response options are under-capturing an experience the open text renders vividly. For product design, the priority is a simple, proactive claim-status communication loop and explicit dependent-coverage explanation at enrolment, with disability-inclusive follow-up given the higher event rate and higher reported friction in PWD households."]}The evidence pack flags a genuine divergence between outcome and experience, and it deserves to be named rather than smoothed over. A female client in Rwanda said, "I didn't get full guidance and support on the documents submitted," and another reported, "I wasn't know that my grandchild is not supposed to get medical care from my insurance" — a coverage-scope misunderstanding discovered only at the point of claim. A female client in Uganda described the silence that follows submission: "She shared her documents with the officer, but there has been no feedback from him or the insurance providers." A female client in Malawi asked plainly, "I want the officer to come and help us to process the insurance claims because she promised to assist us." These accounts sit alongside very low structured challenge codes — only 1.6% of women and 3.4% of men network-wide flagged difficulty knowing claim status — which suggests the closed-response options are under-capturing an experience the open text renders vividly. For product design, the priority is a simple, proactive claim-status communication loop and explicit dependent-coverage explanation at enrolment, with disability-inclusive follow-up given the higher event rate and higher reported friction in PWD households.
